opus-5.5.text:
I think in the long run, yes, almost certainly. When you cut off a country with China's resources and engineering talent from the best hardware, you're essentially creating a guaranteed domestic market for whoever can build the substitute. Before the export controls, a Chinese lab choosing between NVIDIA and a Huawei Ascend chip would just pick NVIDIA every time: better software, CUDA, the whole ecosystem. Now that choice is being made for them, and that kind of forced demand is exactly what an infant industry needs to mature.

But I'd separate the short term from the long term. In the near term, the restrictions clearly hurt. Training frontier models is a compute game, and Chinese labs have been operating with less of it. You see that in how they talk: the DeepSeek folks have been pretty open that compute is their binding constraint. Some of the impressive efficiency work coming out of China, like clever mixture-of-experts architectures and low-level optimizations, is partly a product of that scarcity. Constraints breed creativity, but they're still constraints.

The hard part for China isn't really chip design. They have good designers. It's manufacturing: getting to leading-edge process nodes without EUV lithography, and things like high-bandwidth memory, which is a real bottleneck. SMIC has pushed further on older tools than a lot of people expected, but yields and volume matter enormously when you need hundreds of thousands of accelerators. And then there's software. CUDA's moat is years of developer tooling, and rebuilding that takes time even with a captive market.

So my honest take is that the controls buy time rather than permanently stopping anything. They slow China down during what might be a really important window for AI, and the policy bet is that the window matters. The cost of that bet is that you've probably accelerated a domestic Chinese chip ecosystem that, five or ten years out, will be more capable and more independent than it otherwise would have been. Whether that tradeoff is worth it depends a lot on how fast you think AI progress is going to be over the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's pretty clear at this point that the restrictions are accelerating domestic chip development, and honestly I think that was always going to be the outcome. When you cut off a country's access to the best hardware, you don't make them stop wanting it, you just make them build it themselves. Huawei's Ascend line is the obvious example. A couple years ago people were pretty dismissive of it, and now you see DeepSeek and other labs doing real work on it, and the Chinese government is actively pushing companies to buy domestic.

The thing I'd push back on a little is the framing that this makes China catch up right away. The hard part isn't designing a chip, it's manufacturing it at scale and building the software stack around it. CUDA is a huge moat. NVIDIA's ecosystem has had fifteen-plus years of people writing kernels and tuning libraries, and that's not something you replicate in two or three years. And on the fab side, without access to the most advanced lithography, you're stuck a generation or two behind, and you're taking yield hits that make every chip more expensive.

So the way I think about it is: the export controls probably slow China down in absolute terms over the next few years, but they also guarantee that in five to ten years there's a mature, independent Chinese chip ecosystem that doesn't need NVIDIA at all. Whether that trade was worth it is really a policy question, not a technical one. From the open model side, which is where I spend most of my time, what I notice is that the Chinese labs have gotten extremely good at doing more with less. DeepSeek's efficiency work was partly a response to compute constraints. So in some ways the restrictions have pushed the research in directions that are actually pretty useful for everyone.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll spur investment in domestic chips, but that’s different from saying they’ll produce something better than NVIDIA. If you can’t buy the hardware you want, you have a much stronger incentive to build an alternative, and Chinese AI companies have a stronger incentive to use it, even if it’s initially less capable.

The hard part is that this isn’t just a chip problem. It’s manufacturing, memory, networking, and the software that makes thousands of chips work together reliably. You can put a lot of money into that, but it takes time to build.

So both things can be true: restrictions can slow China’s AI development in the near term, and they can accelerate the development of a domestic ecosystem over the longer term. Whether that ultimately produces better chips is much harder to predict.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they create a much stronger incentive to develop domestic chips, but incentive and capability are different things. If you can buy NVIDIA GPUs, it’s hard to justify taking a risk on a domestic alternative. If you can’t, suddenly there’s a customer willing to work through the problems with you.

But the challenge isn’t just designing a chip. It’s manufacturing it, getting enough memory, connecting thousands of chips together, and building software that makes them useful. NVIDIA has a very strong ecosystem around all of that, and replacing it takes time.

So, yes, restrictions could accelerate China’s domestic chip industry while also slowing its AI development in the near term. Those outcomes can both be true. The harder question is whether that longer-term push toward self-sufficiency outweighs the immediate constraints, and I don’t think we can confidently answer that yet.
